newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: S&P lowers Telecom rating to AA from AA+.
newsitem.headline: S&P lowers Telecom rating to AA from AA+.

text.p: Ratings agency Standard and Poor's on Friday said it had lowered its long term rating of Telecom Corp of New Zealand to 'AA' from 'AA+'.
S&P also said it had removed Telecom from creditwatch-negative, where it was placed on November 14, 1996, and affirmed Telecom's short term 'A-1+' rating.

At the same time, S&P said it had lowered its ratings on Telecom Corp of New Zealand (Overseas Finance) Ltd and TCNZ Finance Ltd, both guaranteed subsidiaries of TCNZ, to 'AA' from 'AA+', and also removed these ratings from creditwatch.

"This rating action follows TCNZ's decision to externally finance a NZ$1 billion share repurchase programme, continued downward pressure on margins, and uncertainty over TCNZ's multi-media investments," S&P said in a statement.
"TCNZ, nevertheless, continues to maintain a commanding market position in each of its major business segments, which provide the company with reasonably robust cash flows."
S&P said TCNZ had proven to be a strong competitor in one of the world's most deregulated telecommunications markets.
"The outlook is stable," S&P said, adding that Telecom's "strong and diverse revenue base provides a fundamental strength to the ratings, and this is not expected to change in the medium term".

On February 14 1996, TCNZ announced it planned to commence, in February 1997, the repurchase of up to NZ$1 billion of its shares over a one-year period. At that time, TCNZ had yet to announce the precise method of financing the share repurchase.

"Despite a strong market position that generates considerable cash flows, Standard and Poor's estimates that the external financing of the share repurchase will reduce TCNZ's adjusted pretax interest coverage ratios to a low point of about six times, and funds from operation coverage ratios to a low point of about seven times in the next two years," S&P said.

"While these ratios are expected to improve thereafter, the improvement may be slow, reflecting more effective competition and associated margin contraction in many traditional areas of TCNZ's operations.
